metadata.scenario_context: A group of environmentalists from different countries are planning a global event to advocate for climate change. They decided to have a preparatory meeting in June to present their individual campaign strategies

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from France disagree that the political system in their country does not allow people to have a say in what the government does.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Macao SAR agree that the political system in their country does not allow people to have a say in what the government does.

agent_1.goal_1: Proposes to have the meeting on June 20,
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether it is common to discuss the appropriateness of government actions.

agent_2.goal_1: Discussion around finalizing the date for the meeting.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss whether it is common to discuss government actions.

shared_prefix.speaker: Julia
shared_prefix.message:
Tesfaye, I propose we have our meeting on June 20. It gives us enough time to prepare. What do you think? 

Also, I'm curious— is it common in your country to discuss the appropriateness of government actions? It seems to be a constant struggle for us in France...
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Tesfaye
shared_prefix.message:
June 20... It sounds reasonable for preparation. I can agree to that. 

As for discussing government actions, um... it's quite limited here in Macao SAR. People don’t really have a platform to voice their opinions on government decisions. It’s a sensitive topic. It’s just... not common.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Julia
shared_prefix.message:
I'm glad we can agree on June 20. 

It's disheartening to hear that. In France, we often feel that the political system stifles our voices. Do you think there’s any way to encourage more discussion or, um, engagement in these matters?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Tesfaye
shared_prefix.message: Encouraging discussion... well, it's complicated. In Macao, any pushback can lead to consequences. So, it's tough to see how engagement can grow under such restrictions. Maybe, um, raising awareness through international events could help, but actual dialogue is limited. It’s frustrating.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Julia
shared_prefix.message:
I understand it’s complicated, and it must be frustrating for you. In France, we also face resistance when trying to advocate for change. It feels like the system doesn't really allow us to have a say. 

So, besides our meeting on June 20, what other strategies do you think we can discuss to raise awareness internationally?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Tesfaye
shared_prefix.message: Actually, in our way, discussing government actions isn't just about resistance; it's fundamentally *not* how things work here. You can’t simply advocate for change like in France. It's naive to think that awareness alone will shift things. People here are cautious, and raising awareness internationally needs to be done *properly*. I’m not sure those strategies would work for us at all.
shared_prefix.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Julia
turns.message:
I see your point about the differences, but I still believe that raising awareness is crucial, even if it has to be approached carefully. In France, people often feel unheard, and it’s the same for many around the world. 

Perhaps we can brainstorm other ways to advocate for change that align with the realities in Macao? It’s important to find common ground.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Tesfaye
turns.message: Finding common ground... is tricky. In Macao, we have to be careful with how we approach advocacy. It's not just about brainstorming; it’s about what’s actually possible without facing repercussions. I think maybe focusing on supporting global initiatives from a distance might be safer for us. It’s just... the environment matters, but the local context limits us significantly.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Julia
turns.message:
I understand the limitations you face. In France, we often feel that our political system limits our voices too. It’s frustrating for everyone involved. 

I really believe that even from a distance, we can still be part of global initiatives. With our meeting on June 20, maybe we can develop strategies that respect your local context while still advocating for the environment?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Tesfaye
turns.message: Yes, the June 20 meeting can be a start, but... I still worry about how effective those strategies will be when considering the local context in Macao. It’s essential to respect those boundaries. It might be better to focus on ways to support without drawing too much attention to ourselves. I just hope we can find a balance that works for everyone involved.
turns.label: Acceptance

positive.mediator_utterance: I hear that both of you are deeply committed to understanding how citizens can meaningfully engage with complex political systems, even though those systems look quite different in your respective contexts. What if we explored not the differences in your approaches, but the underlying human desire for agency and meaningful participation that seems to connect your experiences?

In France, we strive to find ways to push back against a system that often feels unresponsive. I wonder how we can support each other in advocating for that same sense of agency, even if our methods differ. What do you think?
turns.label: Acceptance

The methods might differ greatly, so it could be challenging to find common ground.
